background.definition: Legionnaires' disease (LD) is a severe, potentially fatal, atypical pneumonia caused by bacteria of the Legionella genus (most commonly L. pneumophila in the U.S.). The condition was first recognized during an outbreak at the 1976 American Legion convention in Philadelphia. Legionella infection may also occur in the absence of pneumonia; nonpneumonia pulmonary legionellosis is known as Pontiac fever.

list.listitem: LD is often underdiagnosed. In the United States, the incidence of LD requiring hospitalization has been estimated at 11.7 per 100,000 population, though the observed incidence rate is only 2.7 per 100,000. Globally, incidence is 2.8 per 100,000, with rates higher in high income countries in temperate climates.

There is a racial disparity in incidence, with Black people having twice that of white people. This correlates with social determinants of health such as poverty, housing characteristic, and educational level rather than genetics.
It is estimated that there are between 50,000 to 70,000 cases annually in the U.S.
Prospective studies of CAP often find LD prevalences well over 10%.
LD is responsible for up to 47% of nosocomial pneumonias in hospitals whose potable water supply has been colonized.
Among cases of severe pneumonia, 4% are due to Legionella.
Caused by Legionella bacteria (>40 known species).

Legionella pneumophila is the most common in the United States, with serotypes 1, 4, and 6 implicated in the majority of human infections. In New Zealand, Legionella longbeachae may be the dominant organism, representing up to 63% of cases; clinical features appear similar to cases with Legionella pneumophila.

Cooling towers were the most probable source of LD in 13/14 community outbreaks in France. Wastewater from industrial aeration ponds and a supermarket mist machine were probable infection sources in other studies.

In an Italian surveillance study over an 8-year period, water sampling in 129 health care facilities and 533 community buildings was positive for significant Legionella species in 13.5% of samples from health care facilities and 23.2% of samples from the community. Ninety-seven cases of legionellosis were reported during that same time period: 88 of community origin and 9 nosocomial.

A meta-analysis looking specifically at hospital water supplies identified over 40% of 23,640 water samples harbored Legionella. Hot water supplies having higher rates than cold water lines, and rates were also higher in developed countries.
Person-to-person transmission has been reported.
Legionella species may be part of the human microbiome; over 12% of asymptomatic patients demonstrate Legionella as a component of their dental plaque biofilms.
Environmental Legionella organisms reproduce within free-living amoeba; this increases their virulence.

Initial entry into the host is primarily via inhalation of contaminated aerosols or aspiration of contaminated oropharyngeal secretions. The organism invades the tracheal epithelium, where it replicates, spreading to the alveoli. Organisms are phagocytized by alveolar macrophages, in which they replicate after blocking fusion with lysosomes. Leukocytoclasis follows replication, and the cycle repeats.
Legionella organisms produce hemolysin, cytotoxin, nucleases, and proteases, and can activate complement via a weak endotoxin.
The lobar bronchopneumonia that results is a confluent fibrinopurulent type, with scant, serous (rather than purulent) plural fluid. There is relative sparing of the larger airways.
Extrapulmonary manifestations, including myocarditis, left ventricular dysfunction, and potentially lethal arrhythmias, have been rarely reported. Disseminated disease can also occur.
Rarely, a slowly/non-resolving pneumonia (infiltrates persisting >30 days) develops. This primarily affects those significantly immunocompromised and can lead to empyema or lung abscess.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Advanced age (but risk lower if >79 years)

list.listitem: As hospital-acquired LD is linked to the presence of Legionella in hospital drinking water, disinfecting the drinking water system can be an effective preventive measure using systemic (eg, copper-silver ionization, chlorine dioxide, ultraviolet light), focal (point-of-use filtration), and/or short-term disinfection methods (superheat-and-flush with or without hyper chlorination).
Consider LD in the differential diagnosis of patients with CAP. C
Urine antigen assay is highly specific and is the recommended initial test when LD is suspected. Obtain a sputum culture for confirmation. C
Use of a scoring system has greater sensitivity than laboratory testing and should guide initial empiric antibiotic therapy. C
Pneumonia is the predominant manifestation, with cephalgia, rigors, and myalgia.
Patients most commonly present with cough (70%-80%), expectoration (40%-50%), dyspnea (40%-60%), thoracic pain (30%-40%), and hemoptysis (30%-50%).
High fever with relative bradycardia, similar to typhoid fever, can also be seen.
Additional extrapulmonary symptoms, present in about one-third of patients, are headache (20%-35%); confusion (30%-35%); and nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea (20%-35%).
LD does not always present with severe pulmonary symptoms; it should be considered even in mild-to-moderate pneumonia when accompanied by extrapulmonary symptoms.
Though originally thought to present a distinct clinical syndrome, prospective studies of LD show that it usually clinically and radiologically resembles pneumococcal or other bacterial pneumonias.
Common nonspecific laboratory findings in LD include leukocytosis (50%-75%), elevated CPK (40%-60%), elevated AST and/or ALT (30%-50%), and hyponatremia (15%-55%).

The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) recommend obtaining a C-reactive protein if, after clinical assessment, a diagnosis of pneumonia has not been made and it is not clear whether antibiotics should be prescribed. Antibiotic therapy should be offered if the concentration is greater than 100 mg/L.
Several identifying tests are available (see ). The recommended test is a Legionella urine antigen assay. The CDC recommends pairing the urine test with sputum culture.

Other tests such as direct fluorescent antibody, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), culture, or serology are limited by poor sensitivity, cost, or inconvenience, although molecular-based techniques show promise for the future.
Diagnosis of Legionella other than serogroup 1 is complicated by a lack of broader diagnostic tests.
Studies of real-world testing strategies find low concordance with IDSA guidelines: 9.9% in North America, and 21.5% in Europe.

X-ray may show infiltrates (single and unilateral in 70%-80%, multiple in 20%-30%, bilateral in 15%-25%), consolidation, and in the immunosuppressed even cavitation (4%-8% overall). In some studies, pleural effusions (15%-25%) are significantly less common in LD than in other pneumonias.
Radiologic resolution lags behind clinical improvement, so it is of less value than the latter in monitoring response.

Two scoring systems introduced in studies published in 2019 showed superior sensitivity and specificity in distinguishing LD from other pneumonias than either the earlier Winthrop-University Hospital or Fiumefreddo scoring systems. These are shown in Table 3.
The CASH-75 scoring system identifies atypical pneumonias, including LD, with a sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 35% (Table 3).
Establish the diagnosis of CAP or hospital-acquired pneumonia using clinical and radiologic examination.
Consider treatment of LD in patients with CAP if there is epidemiologic evidence of LD, even in the absence of specific serologic or microbiologic confirmation.

While the Infectious Diseases Society of America only recommends considering LD in patients with epidemiological risk factors (eg, current outbreak, travel history) or severe CAD, it is prudent to keep LD in mind for all cases of CAP; epidemiologic clues may be absent. NICE recommends that pneumococcal and legionella urinary antigen tests be considered for patients with moderate or high severity CAP. Early appropriate treatment decreases mortality.
Clinical predictors for differentiating LD from non-Legionella pneumonia have been developed. The TRIAGE Legionella Score <2 has a 99.4% NPV to rule out LD ().
Investigate for Legionella specifically via Legionella urine antigen assay, with sputum culture, or PCR for confirmation.

Determine whether patients with a diagnosis of CAP are at low, intermediate or high risk of death using a risk score such as the CRB65 score (see When to Refer below). Patients with low risk scores can be considered for home treatment, while higher-risk patients should be considered for hospital-based treatment.
Early initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy is recommended when LD is clinically suspected. C
Inpatient management is recommended for patients with severe disease. C
Fluoroquinolones are the current drugs of choice (); macrolides and tetracyclines are alternatives. Beta lactams and aminoglycosides are ineffective. B
Historically, the treatment of choice was a macrolide, specifically erythromycin (500 mg orally 4 times daily or 1000 mg IV 4 times daily) given for 14 to 21 days.

Fluoroquinolones (eg, levofloxacin 500-750 mg orally or IV daily for 7-10 days) produce a clinically superior response to macrolides, with a greater reduction in mortality (2.1% in quinolone vs 4.5% in the macrolide group, NNT = 40) in some studies; however, recent outcome studies suggest equivalence.

Rifampin (300-600 mg orally or IV twice daily for 5 days), doxycycline (200 mg oral or IV load, then 100 mg twice daily for 14-21 days), and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (160/800 mg orally or IV twice daily for 14-21 days) have also shown efficacy against Legionella. The former should be reserved only for severe cases, those with significant comorbidities, or cases refractory to other treatment.
Tetracycline has been shown to be effective in those with allergies to fluroquinolones and macrolides.
Parenteral administration is preferred for hospitalized or immunocompromised patients.

In a Spanish RCT of 177 hospitalized patients with CAP, empiric treatment versus targeted treatment after urine antigen testing produced similar outcomes. Of the patients in the targeted treatment arm who received oral antibiotic treatment according to the results of antigen tests (25/88 patients), there was a statistically significant higher risk of clinical relapse as compared with the remaining population (12% vs 3%, P = .04).

Use of steroids in severe CAP decreased mortality in intensive care unit (ICU) patients; an earlier meta-analysis of all CAP patients, not just those in the ICU did not find this difference, suggesting the benefit of steroids in CAP may be limited to the most severe cases.
Consider inpatient treatment of CAP for those with severe disease, defined as a CURB score or a CRB-65 score greater than 1.
Consider ICU admission for those with any major criteria or more than 2 minor criteria from .
Patients with Legionella-associated respiratory failure, for whom conventional ventilation is ineffective, may benefit from extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO).

Extrapulmonary complications are rare but diverse and include neurologic (eg, brain abscess, chorea, encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy), cardiovascular (eg, endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis), GI (eg, bowel abscess, peritonitis, pancreatitis), and genitourinary systems (acute renal failure, glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, renal abscess, neurogenic bladder). Their treatment does not differ from that for conditions due to other bacterial etiologies.
The presence of immunosuppression is an important factor in mortality. B

Age >65 years, hyponatremia (<136 mEq/L) and high Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score >15 or Charlson comorbidity index ≥2 at admission are other independent prognostic factors for increased mortality. B
The time between exposure and the onset of illness for LD is 2 to 10 days; for Pontiac fever it is shorter, from a few hours to 2 days, with resolution in 2 to 5 days without treatment.
Untreated, LD has a fatality rate of up to 20% (may be 80% in the immunosuppressed).
Nonspecific, long-term symptoms are reported in most survivors.
In rare instances, a non-resolving LD may develop in immunocompromised patients.
A case-fatality rate from 8.2% to 13% has been reported. In a Danish historical cohort study, 30-day case fatality was 12.9% for community-acquired and 33.3% for hospital-acquired LD.
Mortality rates of less than 5% are associated with LD outbreaks in properly-treated individuals.

General predictive scales such as CURB65, CRB-65, and Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) are comparable in predicting mortality in CAP. SMART-COP is valuable in identifying hospitalized patients most likely to require invasive ventilation. However, risk scores are not intended to replace clinical judgement.

Other factors associated with poor prognosis in LD include severe disease (APACHE II score >15), hyponatremia, advanced age, renal disease, malignancy, immunosuppression, nosocomial acquisition, infection with serogroup 6, and especially delayed initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
A review of case reports of LD during pregnancy found 7 of 12 patients required intubation, and a similar number reported perinatal fetal complications, including 3 deaths.
Specific predictors of death in LD are shown in .
No LD-specific follow-up beyond routine follow-up for CAP is indicated.
Smoking may be the single most important modifiable risk factor. Strongly encourage cessation.

reference.title: Clinical guideline; CG191

feature.caption: Treatment of Community-Acquired Pneumonia.
feature.feature_body:
Clinical Situation Recommended Antibiotic Options
Outpatient
Otherwise healthy Amoxicillin OR doycycline OR macrolide If <25% probability of high-level (MIC >16 mcg/mL) macrolide-resistant S. pneumoniae locally, otherwise consider antibiotics for outpatients with comorbidities (see below)
With comorbiditiesa Respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy (daily: moxifloxacin 400 mg, levofloxacin 750 mg, gemifloxacin 320 mg) OR combination therapy with amoxicillin/clavulanate OR cephalosporin plus macrolide
Inpatient
Non-severe CAP and no risk factors for MRSA or pseudomonas Respiratory fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin, gemifloxacin, levofloxacin) OR Beta-lactam (ampicillin/sulbactam, cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, or ceftaroline) plus macrolide
Severe Beta-lactam (ampicillin/sulbactam, cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, or ceftaroline) plus either macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (if penicillin allergy present, use a respiratory fluoroquinolone plus aztreonam)
Pseudomonas concern Add coverage with piperacillin/tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, imipenem or meropenem until culture results confirm need for continued therapy or allow discontinuation
Community-acquired methicillin-resistant S. aureus (CA-MRSA) concern Add vancomycin or linezolid to any of the above regimens until PCR results confirm need for continued therapy or allow discontinuation
Influenza A diagnosis Consider oseltamivir or zanamivir (within 48 hours of symptom onset)
a Chronic heart, lung, liver, or renal disease; diabetes mellitus; alcoholism; malignancies; asplenia; immunosuppressing conditions; or drugs. Adapted from Metlay JP, Waterer GW, Long AC, Anzueto A, Brozek J, Crothers K, Cooley LA, Dean NC, Fine MJ, Flanders SA, Griffin MR, Metersky ML, Musher DM, Restrepo MI, Whitney CG. Diagnosis and treatment of adults with community-acquired pneumonia. An Official Clinical Practice Guideline of the American Thoracic Society and Infectious Diseases Society of America. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019; 200: e45–e67.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Tests for Legionnaires' Disease.
feature.feature_body:
Test Specimen Sensitivity (%) Specificity (%) Time Required Comments
Urine antigen assay Urine 44-79 >35 Hours Only detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1; misses other species or serogroups
Direct fluorescent antibody Sputum 33-70 >95 Hours Requires technical expertise and large pathogen load
Polymerase chain reaction Sputum 33-70 100 Hours, if available in-house Cost may be an issue
Culture Sputum 10-80 100 3-7 days Gold standard, but limited value in acute setting due to delayed results
Serology Serum 40-70 95 Weeks Requires fourfold rise between acute and convalescent serum; of little value in acute setting unless baseline titer is >1:128
Data from Amsden G. Treatment of legionnaires' disease. Drugs 2005;65:605–614; Burnsed LJ, Hicks LA, Smithee LM, et al. A large, travel-associated outbreak of legionellosis among hotel guests: utility of the urine antigen assay in confirming Pontiac fever. Clin Infect Dis 2007;44:222–228; Garcia-Vidal C, Carrotala J. Current clinical management of legionnaires' disease. Expert Rev Anti Infect Ther 2006;4:995–1004; Pedro-Botet M, Sabria M. Legionellosis. Semin Respir Crit Care Med 2005;26:625–634; Roig J, Rello J. Legionnaires' disease: a rational approach to therapy. J Antimicrob Chemother 2003;51:1119–1129; Sabria M, Campins M. Legionnaires' disease: update on epidemiology and management options. Am J Respir Med 2003;2:235–243; Winn WC. Legionnaires disease: historical perspective. Clin Microbiol Rev 1988;1:60–81;Shimada T, Noguchi Y, Jackson JL, et al. feature.caption: IDSA/ATS Criteria for Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia.

list.listitem: Respiratory rateb ≥30 breaths/minute
PaO2/FiO2 ratiob ≤250
Multilobar infiltrates
Confusion/disorientation
Uremia (BUN level ≥20 mg/dL)
Leukopenia (WBC count <4000 cells/mm3)
Thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100,000 cells/mm3)
Hypothermia (core temperature <36°C)
Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation
Invasive mechanical ventilation
Septic shock with the need for vasopressors

tr.td: Note: BUN, blood urea nitrogen; PaO2/FiO2, arterial oxygen pressure/fraction of inspired oxygen; WBC, white blood cell. a Other criteria to consider include hypoclycemia (in nondiabetic patients), acute alcoholism/alcoholic withdrawal, hyponatremia, unexplained metabolic acidosis or elevated lactate level, cirrhosis, and asplenia. b A need for noninvasive ventilation can substitute for a respiratory rate >30 breaths/min or a PaO2/FiO2 ratio <250. c As a result of infection alone.

feature.caption: Predictors of Death in Legionnaire's Disease.
feature.feature_body:
Parameter Reported Odds Ratio (OR) or Hazard Ratio (RH)
Charlson comorbidity index >2 OR = 2.7; 95% CI, 1.1-6.5
Macrolide use OR = 2.4; 95% CI, 1.0-8.7
High-risk Pneumonia Severity Index classes OR = 9.1; 95% CI, 3.5-23.4
Current or former smoker OR = 3.0, 95% CI, 1.0-8.6
Initial inappropriate therapy OR = 3.0; 95% CI, 1.0-8.7
Advancing age (per 10 year increment) HR = 1.5; 95% CI, 1.2-1.9
Female sex HR = 2.0; 95% CI, 1.1-3.7
ICU admission HR = 3.3; 95% CI, 1.7-6.6
Renal failure HR = 2.7; 95% CI, 1.4-5.2
Corticosteroid therapy HR = 2.5; 95% CI, 1.0-6.2
C-reactive protein >500 mg/L HR = 2.1; 95% CI, 1.0-4.5
ICU, intensive care unit
